messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Priya had been seven when the physical force first settled into the architecture of her life. Her caregiver’s hands, heavy and unyielding, would descend without warning, the sharp crack of a wooden chair leg striking her shoulder echoing through their sunlit California living room. What frightened her most was not the pain itself, but the absolute calm with which it was administered and the way the adults in the room simply nodded, as though such force were a natural order. No one held anyone accountable; the caregiver faced no consequences, and the household settled back into its rhythm. Priya had come to believe that the world operated on an unspoken rule of endurance, that she had simply been marked for this treatment. Over the following decades, she learned to navigate a life of quiet readiness. Working as a photographer, she spent her days behind viewfinders and lenses, often in studios or traveling to galleries across the West Coast. Her profession demanded an outward gaze, but inwardly she remained on guard all the time, her eyes tracing the corners of rooms, her shoulders held slightly forward. When the darkroom’s developing tray clanged against the sink, or when a sudden voice rose above the usual hum in a crowded studio, her hands would rise automatically to cover her face. She tried hard to control her emotions, smoothing her expression until the moment passed, yet beneath the composed surface, the memory remained, sometimes sharp and sometimes just out of reach. When she tried to deliberately remember what happened, she found it difficult to access the memory, as though it floated just beyond the glass of her awareness. But when it did surface, the shame on recall was immediate and heavy, a hot rising in her chest, and the terror on recall felt identical to the childhood experience, as if the past had simply paused and was waiting for her to notice. She spent years asking why the event had happened to her, turning the circumstances over in her mind, searching for meaning in the patterns of her choices and her relationships. Her avoidance of crowded spaces became a steady habit, formed over weeks and months, until she preferred the solitary control of her converted warehouse studio. She had stopped attending family gatherings in the Bay Area, finding the familiar rhythms of South Asian kinship increasingly distant. Her divorce had been quiet, a gradual drifting rather than a rupture, and she no longer belonged anywhere, suspended between places, between past and present, between the woman she was and the woman the world expected her to be. The consequences accumulated quietly: she turned down collaborative assignments, worked longer hours alone, and let her professional network thin until the studio walls felt both protective and isolating. What finally brought her to the clinic was the realization that her guard had become a permanent fixture. At seventy, she sat in a sunlit waiting room, her hands resting in her lap, her eyes scanning the door, the clock, the faces of the other patients. She was certain that the world still demanded the same unyielding endurance, that no accountability had ever truly been rendered for what was done to her. She sought help not to erase the past, but to understand it, hoping that somewhere in the quiet space between memory and meaning, she might finally find a place where she could rest her hands and simply breathe.
